item.title: Crystal structures of tetraketide synthase reveal the mechanistic basis for partitioning products in cannabinoid biosynthesis
item.dc:creator: Kristofer R. Gonzalez-DeWhitt
Cameron W. Flowers
Natalia Ermolova
Anthony N. Farina
Jeff Abramson
item.description:
Authors: Kristofer R. Gonzalez-DeWhitt, Cameron W. Flowers, Natalia Ermolova, Anthony N. Farina, Jeff Abramson
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Tetraketide synthase (TKS), a plant type III polyketide synthase, catalyzes the iterative condensation of hexanoyl-CoA and three malonyl-CoAs to generate a linear tetraketide-CoA that is cyclized to olivetolic acid (OA), an essential intermediate in cannabinoid biosynthesis. TKS also produces abundant tri- and tetraketide lactones that divert flux from OA. Here, we report crystal structures of TKS in complex with mono-, di-, tri-, and tetraketide intermediates that reflect relevant catalytic states in substrate loading, chain elongation, and cyclization. Met187 acts as a dynamic steric gate governing substrate tolerance and elongation, while adjacent residues maintain intermediates in an extended, linear conformation. Ser332-mediated interactions promote lactonization through C5-O-C1 ring closure, implicating lactonization as an enzyme-controlled process. Recapture-versus-release of the tetraketide intermediate determines whether linear or cyclized products are formed. These findings establish a framework for engineering TKS variants with improved OA production and advance chemoenzymatic methods for producing cannabinoids and structurally diverse polyketides.

item.title: The human hypothalamus encodes prediction errors during sensory–nutrient inference
item.dc:creator: Putu A. Khorisantono
Fei-Yang Huang
Michael P. F. Sutcliffe
Paul C. Fletcher
I. Sadaf Farooqi
Fabian Grabenhorst
item.description:
Authors: Putu A. Khorisantono, Fei-Yang Huang, Michael P. F. Sutcliffe, Paul C. Fletcher, I. Sadaf Farooqi, Fabian Grabenhorst
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Humans infer the nutrient content of foods from sensory cues, yet the neural and computational basis of these inferences remains unclear. Here we show how oral texture contributes to judgements of fat content by combining purpose-designed foods that dissociated fat from texture with behavioural testing, computational modelling, functional neuroimaging during consumption, and a naturalistic feeding assay. Judgements of fat content reflected established relationships between oral texture and fat and became systematically less accurate when these relationships were violated. A computational model formalized these failures as prediction errors—discrepancies between fat content predicted from texture and actual fat content. During food consumption, the hypothalamus encoded these model-derived prediction errors, responding most strongly when texture predicted more fat than the food contained. Individual differences in hypothalamic sensitivity to texture predicted fat intake during an ad libitum meal. These findings show how sensory inference of fat content engages hypothalamic signals predicting food intake.

item.title: Anyone can be the best depending on how structural variant callers are evaluated
item.dc:creator: Luca Denti
Thomas Krannich
Tomas Vinar
Rayan Chikhi
Paola Bonizzoni
Brona Brejova
Fereydoun Hormozdiari
item.description:
Authors: Luca Denti, Thomas Krannich, Tomas Vinar, Rayan Chikhi, Paola Bonizzoni, Brona Brejova, Fereydoun Hormozdiari
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Structural variants (SVs) are medium- and large-scale genomic alterations that shape phenotypic diversity and disease risk. Numerous methods have been proposed for discovering SVs, however their benchmarking has been inconsistent across studies, often resulting in contradictory findings. We evaluate the performance of several SV discovery methods for detecting unbalanced SVs from long-read sequencing data and observe substantial variation in performance and ranking depending on the choice of ground truth, reference genome, and genomic regions used for evaluation. Our results indicate that these discrepancies largely arise from inconsistencies among SV callsets used as ground truth, ranging from consortium-curated benchmarks to callsets derived from high-quality assemblies. These discrepancies call for additional caution in downstream analyses and in drawing conclusions based on predicted SVs. Our findings underscore the complexity of evaluating SV detection methods and highlight the need for careful consideration and field-standard practices when reporting performance metrics.

item.title: Changing mercury exposure in the Yukon Watershed linked to traditional diet shifts and permafrost thaw
item.dc:creator: M. Isabel Smith
Emily A. Seelen
Edda A. Mutter
Anna R. Godduhn
Marie E. Lowe
John S. Magyar
A. Joshua West
item.description:
Authors: M. Isabel Smith, Emily A. Seelen, Edda A. Mutter, Anna R. Godduhn, Marie E. Lowe, John S. Magyar, A. Joshua West
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11871
Abstract: Abstract Rapid Arctic warming is disrupting ecosystems and traditional subsistence resources, and simultaneously may release toxic mercury into aquatic ecosystems. Together, these changes threaten food security and public health. In the Yukon River Basin of Alaska, many Indigenous communities that traditionally rely on subsistence fishing are facing precipitous declines in salmon populations. Alternative protein sources can contain up to eight times more mercury, with burbot, northern pike, and beluga being major dietary mercury contributors. More reliance on these proteins could increase mercury exposure, while permafrost thaw is projected to increase mercury concentrations in fish by 21–175% by 2100. Here, we combine diet surveys and subsistence harvest data to develop a hypothetical dietary mercury model. Dietary shifts and permafrost-driven increases in fish mercury could increase mercury intake up to 486%, potentially exceeding public health guidelines and highlighting the vulnerability of Arctic food systems to interacting environmental and ecological change.

item.title: Expanding antimicrobial chemical space by engineering drug safety
item.dc:creator: Tahoura Samad
Chayanon Ngambenjawong
Henry Ko
Savan Patel
Cristiana DeAgazio
Heather E. Fleming
Sangeeta N. Bhatia
item.description:
Authors: Tahoura Samad, Chayanon Ngambenjawong, Henry Ko, Savan Patel, Cristiana DeAgazio, Heather E. Fleming, Sangeeta N. Bhatia
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11835
Abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) infections are a major health threat. Although advances in high-throughput screening, genome mining, and machine learning have accelerated antimicrobial discovery, insufficient separation between antibacterial efficacy and host toxicity remains a bottleneck to the clinical development of new antimicrobial compounds. Here, we establish a generalizable, two-component strategy to engineer drug safety and mobilize otherwise inaccessible chemical space for antimicrobial therapy, using calicheamicin, a potent cytotoxin with unacceptable host toxicity, as a proof of concept. First, we engineer a conditionally active drug conjugate that limits calicheamicin activity to infected tissue, thereby reducing systemic toxicity. Second, we engineer a self-resistance enzyme from Micromonospora echinospora , the natural producer of calicheamicin, as a long-circulating antidote to neutralize calicheamicin outside infected tissue, further reducing off-target toxicity. The conjugate exhibits activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens upon exposure to a protease present within the infected microenvironment. When delivered with the antidote, antibacterial efficacy is maintained while off-target toxicity is reduced in mouse models of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pneumonia. We anticipate that our dual strategy, which engineers drug safety rather than selecting for it, provides a generalizable framework for mobilizing promising but toxic compounds as antimicrobials.

item.title: Identification and functional characterization of bacterial bilirubin vinyl reductase across vertebrate gut microbiomes
item.dc:creator: Angela K. Jiang
Maggie R. Grant
Gabriela Arp
Keith Dufault-Thompson
Alexandra M. Clarke
Yue Li
Danielle Lehman
Alan K. Jarmusch
item.description:
Authors: Angela K. Jiang, Maggie R. Grant, Gabriela Arp, Keith Dufault-Thompson, Alexandra M. Clarke, Yue Li, Danielle Lehman, Alan K. Jarmusch, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Gut bacteria reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen, allowing it to be excreted through feces and urine, but studies have long noted a heterogeneous mixture of partially reduced bilirubin-derived intermediates, suggesting that multiple enzymes are involved. Here we identify bilirubin vinyl reductase (BilV), an Old Yellow Enzyme family reductase encoded in the genomic neighborhood of the known bilirubin reductase ( bilR ). Using heterologous expression and LC–MS/MS, we show that BilR acts on the methine bridges in the bilirubin reduction pathway; co-expression with BilV enables vinyl-group reduction and complete conversion to urobilinogen. In bacterial genomes, bilV co-occurs primarily with the bilR -insertion subtype and is largely absent alongside bilR -short. Analysis of 1,197 gut metagenomes across 14 vertebrate species reveals that this differential co-occurrence shapes pathway availability across hosts: carnivores and omnivores carry balanced bilR and bilV , whereas avian microbiomes, dominated by bilR -short, are depleted for bilV . These findings establish that bilirubin reduction to urobilinogen involves two enzymes with complementary regioselectivity, revising the previous model, and that their distribution across vertebrate gut microbiomes varies in relation to host bile pigment chemistry.

item.title: Room-temperature continuous-wave mid-infrared microdisk laser on InP enabled by InAs quantum dots
item.dc:creator: Haotian Zeng
Yangqian Wang
Hui Jia
Jae-Seong Park
Igor P. Marko
Dominic A. Duffy
Mengxun Bai
Yutong Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Haotian Zeng, Yangqian Wang, Hui Jia, Jae-Seong Park, Igor P. Marko, Dominic A. Duffy, Mengxun Bai, Yutong Zhang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Mid-infrared photonics is important for gas monitoring, non-invasive medical diagnostics, and free-space optical links. Realizing high-density photonic integrated circuits in the short-wave mid-infrared (SW-MIR, 2–3 μm) requires compact, efficient microscale lasers that can be integrated on standard platforms. Conventional quantum-well microcavity lasers cannot sustain efficient operation as cavities shrink because lateral carrier diffusion and surface recombination impose a fundamental limit on the threshold, while Auger recombination and thermal carrier leakage losses severely compromise thermal stability in the SW-MIR window. Here, we demonstrate that the strong carrier localization in self-assembled InAs quantum-dot (QD) gain medium circumvents these limitations. A five-stack InAs/InP QD active region achieves room-temperature continuous-wave single-mode lasing in a suspended 5.5 µm microdisk at 2.064 µm. The device also sustains lasing up to 110 °C under pulsed excitation. Temperature-dependent spectra and electronic structure analysis reveal ground-to-excited state dynamics and suppression of thermal carrier leakage. These results demonstrate the potential of QD gain media for compact SW-MIR light sources on InP and Si photonic platforms.

item.title: Sustained changes to urban mobility after COVID-19 reinforced socioeconomic inequalities in Argentina, Chile and Colombia
item.dc:creator: Carmen Cabrera
Miguel González-Leonardo
Andrea Nasuto
Ruth Neville
Francisco Rowe
item.description:
Authors: Carmen Cabrera, Miguel González-Leonardo, Andrea Nasuto, Ruth Neville, Francisco Rowe
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11834
Abstract: Abstract Urban mobility is central to economic activity, social inclusion and access to services. COVID-19 caused disruptions to mobility globally, yet its long-term impacts in Latin America remain poorly understood. Using > 170 million anonymised and aggregated location records from Meta-Facebook users in Argentina, Chile and Colombia (April 2020-May 2022), we examine changes in overall mobility volume relative to pre-pandemic baselines across socioeconomic and rural-urban gradients. Two years after the pandemic onset, mobility in the highest-density urban cores remained ~ 25–50% below baseline across the three countries, while the top 33% most affluent communities had not returned to baseline. These differences are explained by the scale of the initial mobility shock rather than by subsequent recovery rates. Our findings reveal how a global shock can entrench disparities in human mobility, with implications for urban resilience and planning in unequal nations. Our study underscores the need for proactive policies to prevent long-lasting mobility inequalities.

item.title: Development and clinical validation of a multimodal AI framework to predict persistent fever during antibiotic therapy in hospitalized patients with cancer
item.dc:creator: Gernot Pucher
Kevin Kopp
Aman Deep
Anna M. Stark
Marcel Wiesweg
Martin Schuler
Felix Nensa
H. Christian Reinhardt
item.description:
Authors: Gernot Pucher, Kevin Kopp, Aman Deep, Anna M. Stark, Marcel Wiesweg, Martin Schuler, Felix Nensa, H. Christian Reinhardt, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 12040
Abstract: Abstract Among hospitalized cancer patients, persistent fever despite intravenous antibiotics often triggers treatment escalation and additional diagnostics. Earlier identification of patients at low risk for ongoing fever could support more selective decision-making. We developed and compared multimodal AI frameworks to predict persistent fever at the 48–72-hour reassessment window. Models integrated structured variables, time-series, notes, and chest imaging. Models were developed in a University Hospital Essen cohort and evaluated using holdout validation, two pooled regional hospitals, and MIMIC-IV ICU. A feature-level tabularized multimodal TabPFN model showed consistent discrimination, with AUC 0.84 (95% CI, 0.81–0.86) in cross-validation, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.77–0.87) in holdout validation, and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.74–0.81) in MIMIC-IV; other multimodal strategies showed comparable but more variable performance. Performance was primarily driven by temperature dynamics, while chest-radiograph imaging provided no incremental predictive value. In a clinician validation study, the multimodal model outperformed clinicians (Trial 1 balanced accuracy: 0.77 vs 0.60; Trial 2: 0.79 vs 0.57), while clinician balanced accuracy reached 0.71 (95% CI 0.67–0.75) in the AI-assisted condition, suggesting potential benefit of AI support. Overall, multimodal AI demonstrates potential to support 48-hour antibiotic reassessment and stewardship-oriented decision-making, although further prospective studies are needed.

item.title: Bacterial whole-cell biosensors uncover spatially variable sialic acid availability within the inflamed mammalian gut
item.dc:creator: David Carreño
Clare M. Robinson
Raphaella Jackson
Peirong Li
Vanessa Nunes
Susana A. Palma-Duran
Emma Nye
James I. Macrae
item.description:
Authors: David Carreño, Clare M. Robinson, Raphaella Jackson, Peirong Li, Vanessa Nunes, Susana A. Palma-Duran, Emma Nye, James I. Macrae, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Host mucin-derived sialic acids are key drivers of microbial colonisation, growth and pathogenicity within the mammalian gut. However, their study is hindered by complex host-microbiome interactions and rapid metabolite turnover, meaning that conventional measurements of faeces or bulk digesta often fail to capture their local availability. Here, we use an engineered Escherichia coli whole-cell biosensor, based on a NanR-regulated transcriptional circuit, to report in situ sialic acid bioavailability in the inflamed mouse gut. The biosensor robustly colonises the mouse gut and remains functional for at least six weeks. Organ-scale imaging at single-bacterial resolution reveals strong correlations between disease status and biosensor response in two murine inflammation models. Spatial profiling in a murine colitis model further identifies unexpected separation between peak microbial sialic acid sensing and the primary site of host inflammatory injury. Simultaneous tracking of host and microbial inflammatory markers also helps interpret the response to sialidase inhibition, which in this setting accelerates disease recovery. Together, these data reveal complex spatial dynamics of shared host-microbiome metabolism and establish engineered bacterial biosensors as a useful approach for monitoring the in situ bioavailability of rapidly turned-over gut metabolites.

item.title: Learning beyond rigid manipulation with hybrid soft-rigid robots
item.dc:creator: Mariano Ramírez Montero
Ebrahim Shahabi
Giovanni Franzese
Jens Kober
Barbara Mazzolai
Cosimo Della Santina
item.description:
Authors: Mariano Ramírez Montero, Ebrahim Shahabi, Giovanni Franzese, Jens Kober, Barbara Mazzolai, Cosimo Della Santina
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Rigid-soft robot hybrids promise to unite the precision and repeatability of rigid manipulators with the compliance and adaptability of soft structures. Yet, full-fledged rigid-soft manipulators remain largely unexplored, in part because the intelligence required to exploit this combination is still missing. Here, we introduce a hybrid robotic system obtained by the series interconnection of a rigid arm and a soft manipulator, and systematically examine its ability to perform both established and previously inaccessible manipulation tasks. We show that a tailored imitation learning algorithm–generally applicable to this class of hybrid systems–leverages the complementary roles of rigid precision and soft embodiment to acquire manipulation skills and generalize them in a single shot across task variations. As a result, the system matches or exceeds the performance of rigid robots in classical tasks such as stacking, while enabling qualitatively new behaviors, including grasping objects through narrow openings.

item.title: Extending frequency metrology to increasingly complex molecules: SI-traceable sub-Doppler mid-IR spectroscopy of trioxane
item.dc:creator: Dang-Bao-An Tran
Mathieu Manceau

item.description:
Authors: Dang-Bao-An Tran, Mathieu Manceau, Olivier Lopez, Andrey Goncharov, Pierre Asselin, Anne Amy-Klein, Benoît Darquié
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Bringing increasingly complex polyatomic molecules within reach of precision measurement experiments opens new prospects ranging from Earth sciences and astrophysics, to metrology and quantum sciences. Here, we demonstrate sub-Doppler mid-IR spectroscopic measurements of, to our knowledge, the largest molecule to date, 1,3,5-trioxane, (H 2 CO) 3 , in its ν 5 CO stretching mode. To this end, we use an ultra-high-resolution ~10.3 µm spectrometer based on a sub-Hz quantum cascade laser remotely calibrated against state-of-the-art primary frequency standards via a metrology-grade fibre link. We perform saturated absorption spectroscopy at low pressure with ~100 kHz resolution. This allows measuring the absolute frequency of hundreds of rovibrational transitions at unprecedented statistical and systematic uncertainties for such a complex species, as low as 4.6 kHz and 6.2 kHz respectively. In addition to providing new spectroscopic information on trioxane, our work extends frequency metrology methodologies to ever larger molecular systems, confirming the potential of our technologies for bringing increasingly complex species within reach of ultra-precise measurement experiments.

item.title: Disagreements in global urban growth projections amplify uncertainties in deforestation and carbon emissions
item.dc:creator: Xia Liao
Jasper van Vliet
Yuyu Zhou
Yan Liu
Maria Eugenia Correa-Cano
Robert Mangani
Sven Anders
Joseph Awetori Yaro
item.description:
Authors: Xia Liao, Jasper van Vliet, Yuyu Zhou, Yan Liu, Maria Eugenia Correa-Cano, Robert Mangani, Sven Anders, Joseph Awetori Yaro, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Global urbanization is profoundly reshaping 21st-century land systems, yet its future trajectory remains highly uncertain. Existing projections exhibit divergent urban growth patterns even under identical socioeconomic scenarios. Here, by synthesizing six urban growth projections, we reveal substantial disagreements in the extent and location of urban growth by 2100. These disagreements are amplified by land-system feedbacks, driving cross-dataset variation in urban-induced deforestation (1.75–4.91 million km 2 ) through direct forest conversion and indirect cropland displacement, assuming lost production is compensated by cropland expansion elsewhere. The associated emissions exhibit an absolute range of 29 to 76 GtCO 2 by 2100. Across 100 countries, this range accounts for an average of 3% of unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution emission budgets, reaching 26% in specific countries. Our findings establish cross-dataset disagreement as an important source of uncertainty in land and climate assessments, highlighting the need for robust spatial planning across plausible urban futures.

item.description:
Authors: Catarina Candeias, João Lança, Marta Alenquer, Daniela Brás, Carina Valente, Maria João Amorim, Raquel Sá-Leão
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Streptococcus pneumoniae remains a major public health threat despite widespread use of vaccines and antibiotics. Its synergy with influenza A virus (IAV) often leads to secondary bacterial pneumonia, causing significant morbidity and mortality mainly in vulnerable populations such as children under 5 years old and adults over 65 years old. As pneumococcal pneumonia is preceded by nasopharyngeal colonization, preventing colonization represents a promising intervention strategy. This protective effect depends on bacteriocins encoded at the blp1 locus. Among these, Bac2v1 alone or in combination with Bac1 significantly reduces pneumococcal colonization. Notably, Bac2v1 exerts broad, serotype-independent inhibitory activity, impairing the growth of diverse epidemiologically relevant pneumococcal strains. These findings establish two precision-based, serotype-independent approaches to target pneumococcal colonization: using S. mitis F22 Ad as a live biotherapeutic or administering a bacteriocin mixture produced by this strain. Both approaches have the potential to prevent pneumococcal disease and complement existing strategies.

Abstract: Abstract Self-esteem is a cornerstone of mental health across the lifespan. Throughout life, but particularly during adolescence, self-esteem is shaped by social appraisals. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Reversible light control of supramolecular interactions underpins fundamental processes in nature, inspiring artificial molecular devices and adaptive materials. Existing approaches rely on light-modulated interconversion between ground-state species characterized by distinct binding properties. Here, we introduce twisted intramolecular charge transfer (TICT) as an excited-state specific lever to modulate dye–surface adhesion. item.description:
Authors: Robert Wong, Michael H. McCullough, Tianfeng Lu, Shuyu I. Zhu, Geoffrey J. Goodhill
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Neural decoding is a widely-used machine learning technique for investigating how behavior, perception and cognition are represented in neural activity. However without careful application data leakage can occur, where information from the test set contaminates the training set, leading to biased estimates of decoding performance and potentially invalidating biological conclusions. Here we show that leakage can be introduced in neural decoding studies by common supervised and unsupervised preprocessing steps, including dimensionality reduction. We reveal that in some cases leakage can paradoxically decrease decoding performance relative to unbiased estimates, and we provide theoretical analyses explaining how this occurs. We also show that, for autocorrelated neural time series, randomized k-fold cross-validation can dramatically overstate decoding performance. Based on these findings, we provide detailed recommendations for avoiding data leakage in neural decoding.

Abstract: Abstract Elastic inorganic aerogels are highly attractive for weight-sensitive applications in extreme environments, yet integrating high strength, large-strain recoverability and fatigue resistance within a single architecture remains a longstanding challenge. Abstract: Abstract Transcutaneous electrical stimulation can elicit hand movements by activating peripheral nerves and muscles. Here, we present a wearable system integrating programmable constant-current stimulation, a flexible 32-electrode forearm array with full-array active–return routing, and real-time path and parameter updating. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Hotspot-based reference frames are foundational to plate reconstructions yet increasing evidence indicates that individual Pacific hotspots have migrated over time. How the overall motion of Pacific hotspots relates to the evolution of the underlying Pacific basal mantle structure (BMS), the inferred source of Pacific mantle plumes, remains elusive. Here we combine plate reference frame analysis with global mantle flow simulations to quantify the average motion of Pacific hotspots and compare it with the predicted motion of the Pacific BMS. In the models, the coupled BMS-plume migration is driven by greater subduction flux along the northern Pacific than along the southern Pacific between ~80-45 Ma, which generated persistent southward lower-mantle flow. Our results indicate that the average drift of Pacific hotspots is linked to the motion of the Pacific BMS, highlighting dynamic coupling between surface hotspot motion and basal mantle evolution.

Abstract: Abstract Data-driven subtyping of diabetes can be affected by disease duration and treatment. Abstract: Abstract Continuous-wave-pumped optical parametric oscillators (OPOs) provide an exciting avenue to generate coherent radiation at wavelength regions that are difficult to reach by traditional semiconductor optical amplifiers. Abstract: Abstract Osteoclasts are essential for bone remodeling and homeostasis. Their excessive activation drives pathological bone loss disorders such as periodontitis and arthritis. Current osteoclast-inhibiting therapies are limited by adverse effects and poor specificity, underscoring the importance to identify new regulators of osteoclastogenesis. Here, we conducted a pooled CRISPR–Cas9 screen targeting cluster of differentiation (CD) genes to uncover novel modulators of osteoclast differentiation and identified CD300LD, a single-pass transmembrane protein, as a potent driver of osteoclastogenesis. Its function originates from an excitonic absorption band of a dedoped conjugated polymer, which together with low background permittivity induces optical metallicity in the visible. This allows anisotropic nanostructures to exhibit polarization-dependent optical response through localized surface exciton-polariton resonances, rather than plasmons or dielectric Mie resonances. Abstract: Abstract Aortic aneurysm and dissection (AAD) are life-threatening cardiovascular diseases with limited therapeutic options. Our findings identify PAGln is associated with increased risk for AAD and reveal its potential as a therapeutic target.

Abstract: Abstract Klebsiella pneumoniae infections cause hundreds of thousands of deaths annually, yet a licensed vaccine remains elusive. Current strategies targeting capsular polysaccharides and lipopolysaccharides show promise but face limitations due to the complexity of Klebsiella pathogenesis and incomplete understanding of protective immunity. This Review highlights the critical barriers hindering broad protection against K. pneumoniae . We argue that next-generation vaccines require a paradigm shift, integrating antigen discovery, systems immunology and translational models to define conserved protective targets and immune correlates. Abstract: Abstract The GID/CTLH ubiquitin ligase is a multisubunit E3 conserved across eukaryotes. Taken together, our results establish Gid11 as a bona fide GID substrate receptor and highlight GID as a regulator of metabolic transitions.

Authors: Yefan Wang, Peter Nienow, Jaime Otero, Daniel N. Goldberg
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Global glacier recession is driving a rapid increase in the number and volume of ice-marginal lakes, leading to more frequent Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). The long-term impact of GLOFs on glacier dynamics remains poorly understood, including in Greenland, which holds the largest glacial lake volume in the world. Here, using multi-decadal observations from Isortuarsuup Sermia, Southwest Greenland, we reveal that cyclical GLOFs regulate ice sheet motion. We identify a ‘sawtooth’ pattern of ice-dynamics, whereby multi-year acceleration is terminated abruptly by high-magnitude lake-drainage that resets the glacier to a ‘quiescent’ state for several years. The 2022 event exemplifies this process: the near-terminus ice velocity accelerated briefly from a pre-event baseline of ~200 m a −1 to ~1000 m a −1 before dropping to ~50 m a −1 over subsequent years. Each GLOF releases an immense meltwater volume (mean discharge in 2022 ~17000 m³ s −1 ), carving a ~1.5-km-wide, efficient subglacial channel. This channel enables extensive lowering of the subglacial water pressure, increasing ice–bed friction and suppressing ice motion. As climate warming increases GLOF frequency, this powerful negative feedback will modulate ice sheet motion acting as a brake on ice-dynamics at the margins of the Greenland Ice Sheet.

Abstract: Abstract Regulatory T (Treg) cells contribute to skin homeostasis, but the antigenic targets remain unclear. Whilst CD1a is known to present lipid antigens to effector T cells, the possibility of CD1a presentation to Treg cells us not fully understood. Abstract: Abstract A pause in DNA synthesis that occurs when the replisome encounters an obstacle could lead to genome instability. Although important, systematic identification of replication pause sites is challenging due to their low frequency and delocalised nature. Here we present a single-molecule identification of sites of replisome perturbation across a eukaryotic genome using long-read nanopore sequencing. For each single-molecule replication pause we determine the direction of replication, leading/lagging-strand identity, location and approximate duration, and whether the replisome resumed synthesis. Although pauses are largely diffuse over the genome, they are significantly enriched over transcribed features and correlate with transcription and R-loop levels. Transcription-replication conflicts are more numerous when head-on than co-directional. Finally, we identify genomic loci with a strong bias towards leading over lagging strand pauses, consistent with uncoupling of the helicase from polymerase epsilon. As one such locus overlaps with an epigenetically-regulated gene, we suggest that helicase-polymerase uncoupling resulting from replication pausing could trigger epigenetic switching.

Abstract: Abstract Staphylococcus aureus is a human bacterial pathogen with an array of molecular mechanisms to evade the action of antibiotics. Within the organism, efflux pumps provide a first-line defense mechanism, enabling broad multidrug resistance across antibiotic classes and the ability for the organism to evolve target-level resistance mechanisms. NorA is a key efflux transporter in S. aureus responsible for conferring resistance to fluoroquinolones, puromycin, and other cytotoxic compounds. Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 12001
Abstract: Abstract Aneuploidy, resulting from whole-chromosome or segmental gains and losses, is generally detrimental to organismal fitness and is strongly associated with tumorigenesis. While sex chromosome aneuploidies are relatively well tolerated due to dedicated allelic dosage compensation mechanisms, the existence of comparable regulatory processes for autosomes remains debated. Here, we investigate transcriptional responses to autosomal aneuploidy and identify widespread dosage compensation across affected chromosomes. Using high-sensitivity allele-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing of monoclonal cell expansions spanning diverse ploidies and degrees of aneuploidy, we uncover consistent transcriptional compensation of both chromosomal gains and losses. This response operates in a region-specific manner across both complete and segmental aneuploidies, revealing an unexpected flexibility in dosage regulation. We show that chromosome losses are compensated through increased transcriptional burst frequency from the remaining allele. Complementary proteomics analyses demonstrate additional buffering at the protein level, resulting in a substantial, though still incomplete, restoration of stoichiometric balance across autosomal aneuploid chromosomes for both copy number gains and losses. Analyses of cancer transcriptomes confirm that compensatory mechanisms are active in human tumours. Together, our findings establish dosage compensation as a genome-wide and dynamic response to gene dose imbalance. This mechanism extends beyond sex chromosomes, supports transcriptional homeostasis, and represents a fundamental and evolutionarily conserved mode of gene regulation active across species and in aneuploid cancer cells.

Abstract: Abstract Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting 10% of women, characterized by the growth of endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus. This suggests that endometriotic cells possess an epigenetic identity distinct from normal endometrial cells. While most alterations reflect biological mechanisms shared across anatomical sites, distinct signatures exist between lesion types. By harmonizing independent datasets, our study provides a high-resolution molecular map of lesions and strengthens the evidence that DNA methylation drives endometriosis biology.

Abstract: Abstract Ocean-based geochemical CO 2 removal approaches, including ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) and direct ocean removal (DOR), have received attention for their potential to remove billion-ton-scale amounts of CO 2 from the atmosphere. This enables direct quantification of the oceanic fate of ADA perturbations from approaches such as enhanced rock weathering, riverine alkalinity enhancement and accelerated weathering of limestone. item.description:
Authors: Mingzhi Liu, Panagiotis Alkinoos Polychronopoulos, Yiming Xia, Ann-Sophie Oppelt, Ana Marin Navarro, Tzu-Po Chuang, Veronica Zubillaga, Huaitao Cheng, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11914
Abstract: Abstract Neuroblastoma (NB) arises from neural crest-derived cells of the sympathoadrenal lineage, yet how predisposing genetic lesions influence early human development remains poorly understood. Here, we use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models carrying the familial ALK R1275Q mutation to investigate its role during sympathoadrenal differentiation. We show that ALK R1275Q delays lineage maturation and sustains a proliferative progenitor state characterized by elevated ALK signaling and expansion of a Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like population. This SCP-like state persists during differentiation and is reduced by ALK inhibition or CRISPR-based mutation correction. Although ALK R1275Q alone is insufficient to drive tumor formation in vivo, it enhances susceptibility to oncogenic transformation in cooperation with MYCN. Together, these findings support a model in which ALK R1275Q reshapes developmental trajectories by maintaining a proliferative SCP-like progenitor state, thereby creating a permissive cellular context for NB initiation.

Authors: Júlio Belo Fernandes, Diana Vareta, Sónia Fernandes, Cidália Castro, José João Mendes, João Botelho, Vanessa Machado, Alexandre Trindade, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Climate change, emerging infectious diseases and widening inequalities show that the health of people, animals and ecosystems cannot be separated. However, the ideas we use to understand this interdependence and those we use to organise and practise care have largely developed apart. Here we bring together One Health, linking human, animal and environmental health, and person-centred practice, focused on dignity, relationships and meaningful care. We show where they meet, where they clash and what each offers the other, arguing that care without responsibility for animals and ecosystems is incomplete, as is One Health without attention to lived experience.
